events.title: Confiscations for the veterans in Italy
events.summary: Octavian, charged with settling some 40,000 or more veterans of Philippi, confiscated land from eighteen Italian cities, among them Cremona, Mantua, Beneventum and Capua, and many smaller properties. The dispossessed thronged to Rome, Octavian was stoned in the theatre, and Lucius Antonius and Fulvia championed the victims, leading to the Perusine War.
events.detail: The confiscations were the greatest transfer of land in Italy since Sulla and permanently changed the ownership of the countryside: many veterans sold up within a generation, but many settlements took. Virgil's First and Ninth Eclogues give voice to the dispossessed, and ancient biographers claimed (perhaps from the poems themselves) that the poet's own farm near Mantua was seized and restored through Pollio, Varus and Gallus. Propertius and Horace also lost family land.
events.debate: Whether Virgil's family estate was in fact confiscated is debated; the biographical tradition may have been read out of the poems.

events.title: Antony has Arsinoe IV killed at Ephesus
events.summary: At Cleopatra's request Antony had her younger sister Arsinoe IV, who had led the Alexandrians against Caesar and walked in his triumph of 46 before being allowed into sanctuary at the temple of Artemis at Ephesus, dragged from the temple and killed. An octagonal tomb in Ephesus containing a young woman's skeleton has been proposed, contentiously, as hers.
events.debate: The identification of the Octagon at Ephesus with Arsinoe's tomb is widely doubted.

events.title: Sallust's Catiline and Jugurtha
events.summary: Retired from politics after his African governorship, Sallust wrote the Bellum Catilinae (c. 42-41) and Bellum Iugurthinum (c. 41-40), monographs in an archaic, abrupt style modelled on Thucydides and Cato, analysing Rome's decline through ambition and avarice after the fall of Carthage. His Histories (78-67 onward) survive only in fragments and speeches.
events.detail: The paired speeches of Caesar and Cato in the Catiline debate of 5 December 63 became the classic statement of the two political temperaments of the age. Sallust's theme of moral decline (metus hostilis) shaped Livy, Tacitus and every later account of the Republic's fall.

events.title: The Senate names Herod king of Judaea
events.summary: Fleeing the Parthian-backed Antigonus, Herod, son of Antipater, sailed via Alexandria and Rhodes to Rome in winter 40. Antony and Octavian sponsored him in the Senate, which declared him king of Judaea; the consuls led him to the Capitol to sacrifice. He then had to conquer his kingdom.
events.detail: An Idumaean commoner with no Hasmonean blood, Herod owed his crown entirely to Rome. His betrothal to the Hasmonean princess Mariamme, granddaughter of both Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, was meant to supply the legitimacy he lacked. Josephus dates his reign from this grant (40) and also from the capture of Jerusalem (37).

events.title: Parthians install Antigonus in Jerusalem
events.summary: With the Parthian invasion, the Hasmonean Antigonus, son of Aristobulus II, promised Pacorus 1,000 talents and 500 women to be made king. The Parthians took Jerusalem, captured Hyrcanus II and Phasael by treachery; Phasael killed himself and Antigonus cut off Hyrcanus' ears to disqualify him from the high priesthood.
events.detail: Antigonus' coins, the last Hasmonean issue, carry the first depiction of the Temple menorah and shewbread table, with Hebrew legend 'Mattathias the high priest'. Hyrcanus was taken to Babylonia, where the Jewish community honoured him, and returned to Herod's court only to be executed in 30.

events.title: Death of Fulvia at Sicyon
events.summary: Fulvia, who had raised troops for the Perusine War and, according to Martial's epigram from Augustus, provoked Octavian's verse insults, fled to Greece after Perusia; Antony met her at Athens coldly and she died of illness at Sicyon. Her death smoothed the reconciliation at Brundisium.

events.title: Downfall of Salvidienus Rufus
events.summary: At Brundisium Antony revealed that Quintus Salvidienus Rufus, Octavian's boyhood friend and commander in Gaul with eleven legions, had offered to defect. Octavian summoned him to Rome, where the Senate declared him a public enemy; he was executed or killed himself. Agrippa took his place as Octavian's marshal.

events.title: Antony marries Octavia
events.summary: To seal the Treaty of Brundisium, Antony married Octavian's elder sister Octavia, recently widowed by Gaius Marcellus, with the Senate waiving the ten-month mourning period. Coins of Antony at Ephesus showed both their portraits, the first living Roman woman on coinage.

events.title: Sextus Pompey's Neptune coinage
events.summary: Sextus Pompey's Sicilian mint struck denarii proclaiming him 'son of Neptune' and praefectus classis et orae maritimae, with Neptune standing on a ship's prow, the monster Scylla, the Pharos of Messana, and the Catanaean brothers carrying their parents from Etna's lava, an emblem of Sextus' cognomen Pius.

events.title: Octavian's DIVI IVLI F coinage
events.summary: From about 40 Octavian's gold and silver styled him CAESAR DIVI F or IMP CAESAR DIVI IVLI F, pairing his bearded portrait (mourning for Caesar) with the head of the deified Caesar or the star of the comet. 'Imperator' used as a praenomen was his invention.
scholarship: Syme, 'Imperator Caesar: a study in nomenclature', Historia 7 (1958)

events.title: Quintus Labienus Parthicus Imperator
events.summary: Quintus Labienus, son of Caesar's legate and envoy of the Liberators to Parthia, led the Parthian invasion of Roman Asia in 40 and struck aurei and denarii with his own portrait and a saddled Parthian horse, styling himself Q LABIENVS PARTHICVS IMP, 'the Parthian' in the sense of conqueror of, or with, the Parthians.

events.title: Virgil's Eclogues
events.summary: Virgil's ten pastoral poems, composed about 42-39 under the patronage of Pollio and modelled on Theocritus, transpose Greek bucolic into the Italian countryside of the confiscations. The Fourth Eclogue, addressed to Pollio as consul in 40, prophesies the birth of a child who will bring back the golden age.
events.detail: The Eclogues were performed on stage to great acclaim. Tityrus in the First Eclogue thanks a 'god' in Rome, clearly Octavian, for restoring his land, while Meliboeus goes into exile. The child of the Fourth Eclogue was probably intended as a son expected from the marriage of Antony and Octavia (or Pollio's own son); Christian readers from Constantine onward read it as a prophecy of Christ, which made Virgil a quasi-prophet in the Middle Ages and Dante's guide.
events.debate: Identity of the child of Eclogue 4 (Antony and Octavia's expected son, Pollio's son Saloninus or Asinius Gallus, Octavian's expected child by Scribonia) has never been settled.

events.title: Pollio founds the first public library
events.summary: From the spoils of his campaign against the Parthini in Illyricum, Gaius Asinius Pollio restored the Atrium Libertatis and installed in it the first public library in Rome, with Greek and Latin sections and portraits of authors, including the living Varro. Caesar's plan for a library under Varro's direction had died with him.

events.title: Antony and Octavia in Athens
events.summary: Wintering in Athens in 39/38 with Octavia, Antony played the Greek gentleman, attended lectures, and was hailed as the New Dionysus; Octavia was honoured as Athena Polias. Seneca the Elder reports the jest that Antony agreed to marry Athena but demanded a dowry of 1,000 talents.

events.title: Menodorus surrenders Sardinia to Octavian
events.summary: Menodorus (or Menas), Sextus Pompey's freedman admiral, handed over Sardinia and Corsica, three legions and sixty ships to Octavian, who made him an equestrian. Octavian treated it as Sextus breaking the Treaty of Misenum, and war resumed. Menodorus changed sides twice more.

events.title: Agrippa in Gaul and across the Rhine
events.summary: As governor of Gaul, Agrippa suppressed a rising in Aquitania and became the second Roman to cross the Rhine with an army; he resettled the Ubii, at their request, on the left bank, the origin of the Oppidum Ubiorum (Cologne). He declined a triumph because of Octavian's recent naval defeats.
events.locName: Rhine at the land of the Ubii

events.title: Antony besieges Samosata
events.summary: After Ventidius' victory at Gindarus, Antony took over the siege of Antiochus I of Commagene in Samosata, which had sheltered Parthian fugitives; it dragged on, and he settled for 300 talents. Ventidius, suspected of having taken bribes from Antiochus, returned to Rome to triumph over the Parthians, the first Roman to do so.

battle.significance: Ended with a payment instead of a capture.

events.title: Agrippa builds the Portus Julius
events.summary: Preparing for the decisive war against Sextus Pompey, Agrippa cut channels to join Lake Lucrinus and Lake Avernus to the sea near Puteoli, creating a sheltered naval base where 20,000 freed slaves were trained as rowers through the winter of 37/36. Tunnels through the hills, including the Grotta di Cocceio, connected it to Cumae.

events.title: Antony executes Antigonus
events.summary: After Herod and Sosius took Jerusalem, the last Hasmonean king, Antigonus, was sent in chains to Antony at Antioch and, at Herod's request, beheaded, the first king Rome executed with the axe, says Dio. Herod's rule in Judaea now began in earnest.

events.title: Varro's Res rusticae
events.summary: At eighty, Marcus Terentius Varro wrote three books of dialogues on agriculture, livestock and villa husbandry (including aviaries and fishponds) for his wife Fundania, who had bought a farm. It is the main source for the slave-run estate economy of late Republican Italy, with figures on yields, staff and prices.

events.title: Phraates IV murders his father; Monaeses defects
events.summary: Phraates IV succeeded the grieving Orodes II, whom he then murdered along with his brothers. The noble Monaeses fled to Antony, who promised him three Syrian cities and planned an invasion around his knowledge, but Monaeses was lured home by Phraates, possibly as a double agent.

events.title: Octavian's defeat off Tauromenium
events.summary: In August 36 Octavian ferried three legions to Tauromenium, then was caught by Sextus Pompey's fleet and lost most of his ships; he escaped to the mainland almost alone and contemplated suicide. Cornificius' stranded legions marched across Sicily under constant attack to join Agrippa at Mylae.

battle.significance: Octavian's lowest point in the war; Agrippa's Naulochus followed within weeks.

events.title: Destruction of Antony's siege train
events.summary: Antony, hurrying ahead to besiege Phraaspa, left his siege engines, carried on 300 wagons including an 80-foot ram, under Oppius Statianus with two legions. Parthian and Median cavalry annihilated the column, killing 10,000 men and burning the engines; Artavasdes of Armenia then took his cavalry home.

events.title: Octavian receives tribunician sacrosanctity
events.summary: After Naulochus the Senate voted Octavian an ovation, a golden statue on the Rostra, the right to wear the laurel at all times, and the sacrosanctity of a tribune; Octavian announced the remission of arrears of taxes and promised to restore the Republic once Antony returned from Parthia.
events.detail: This was the first element of the tribunician power that became, from 23, the basis of the Principate. A grant to Octavia and Livia of the same inviolability and freedom from guardianship followed in 35.
events.debate: Appian dates the grant to 36, Dio to 36 or 35; whether a fuller tribunicia potestas was given in 30 is debated.

events.title: Octavian's house on the Palatine
events.summary: Octavian bought the house of the orator Hortensius on the Palatine and adjacent properties; after lightning struck part of it he declared the site public and vowed a temple to Apollo there. The modest-looking rooms, with Second Style paintings such as the 'Room of the Masks', were excavated from 1961 onward.

events.title: Execution of Sextus Pompey at Miletus
events.summary: Fleeing to Asia after Naulochus, Sextus Pompey tried to raise forces and negotiate with both Antony and the Parthians; captured by Antony's general Marcus Titius, he was executed at Miletus. Responsibility was disputed between Antony and his governor Plancus. Titius was later hissed out of Pompey's theatre.

events.title: Octavian takes Siscia
events.summary: Campaigning against the Pannonians, Octavian besieged Siscia (Sisak) at the confluence of the Colapis and Savus with a river fleet, took it after thirty days, and made it a base with twenty-five cohorts under Fufius Geminus, a forward post for later wars on the Danube.

battle.significance: Opened the Sava valley route toward the Danube.

events.title: Horace's first book of Satires
events.summary: Horace, a freedman's son who had fought for Brutus at Philippi and was introduced to Maecenas by Virgil and Varius in 38, published his first book of Satires about 35, including the Journey to Brundisium with Maecenas on a diplomatic mission to Antony in 37 and the 'Bore' satire. Maecenas gave him a Sabine farm about 33.

events.title: Octavian wounded at Setovia
events.summary: In the Dalmatian campaign of 34 Octavian was wounded in the knee besieging Setovia; Promona and Synodium had already fallen. The Dalmatae surrendered in 33, returning the standards taken from Gabinius in 48, which Octavian displayed in the Porticus Octaviae.

battle.significance: Completed Octavian's reconquest of the Dalmatian coast.

events.title: Antony seizes Artavasdes of Armenia
events.summary: Blaming Artavasdes II for the failure of 36, Antony invited him to a meeting at Nicopolis, arrested him with his family and his treasure, occupied Armenia, and took the king in silver chains to Alexandria, where he paraded him in a triumphal procession before Cleopatra.
events.detail: The 'triumph' in Alexandria was presented by Octavian's propaganda as Antony giving a Roman rite to a foreign queen. Artavasdes refused to prostrate himself before Cleopatra and was executed after Actium. Antony's coins of 34 proclaim ARMENIA DEVICTA and show Cleopatra as 'Queen of Kings'.

events.title: Cornelius Nepos' Lives
events.summary: Cornelius Nepos of Cisalpine Gaul, friend of Catullus, Cicero and Atticus, published his De viris illustribus, biographies comparing foreign and Roman generals, kings and historians, the earliest surviving Latin biographies. Only the book on foreign generals and the lives of Cato and Atticus survive; Atticus' life was revised after his death in 32.

events.title: Denarii of Antony and Cleopatra
events.summary: A denarius struck about 32, probably at Antioch or Alexandria, shows Antony with ARMENIA DEVICTA and Cleopatra with the legend CLEOPATRAE REGINAE REGVM FILIORVM REGVM, 'of Cleopatra, Queen of Kings and of her sons who are kings'. It is the only Roman silver coin of a foreign queen with a Latin legend.
events.detail: Its unflattering realism (hooked nose, prominent chin for Cleopatra; thick neck for Antony) has done more than any text to shape modern debate about Cleopatra's appearance. Its message, endorsing the Donations, was precisely the one Octavian exploited.

events.title: Antony's legionary denarii
events.summary: To pay his army and fleet before Actium, Antony struck a vast issue of debased denarii showing a galley and a legionary eagle between standards with the name of each legion, LEG II to LEG XXIII plus the praetorian cohorts and the speculatores. They circulated for over two centuries; Marcus Aurelius restruck the type in 168.
events.detail: Lower silver content (about 92 per cent) kept them out of hoards for melting, which is why they are among the commonest Republican coins in hoards of the second century AD. The legion numbers are an invaluable source for Antony's order of battle, though LEG XXIV, XXV and XXX are modern forgeries or misreadings. Pliny notes Antony mixed iron into his denarii.

events.title: The consuls flee to Antony
events.summary: The consuls of 32, Antony's partisans Gaius Sosius and Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, attacked Octavian in the Senate; Octavian appeared with an armed escort, and the consuls and some 300 senators left Rome for Antony at Ephesus. Octavian let them go and summoned the Senate to hear his charges.
events.detail: Augustus later claimed that more than 700 senators fought under his standards at Actium, implying that perhaps a third of the Senate went east. With both consuls in Antony's camp, Octavian's position rested on the oath of Italy rather than on any magistracy, since his triumviral powers had arguably lapsed at the end of 33.

events.title: Agrippa seizes Methone and the Greek coast
events.summary: Early in 31 Agrippa crossed with part of the fleet, stormed Methone in the south-western Peloponnese, where the exiled king Bogud of Mauretania was killed, then took Leucas, Patrae and Corinth, cutting Antony's grain route from Egypt and leaving his army at Actium hungry and stricken by disease.
events.detail: These operations, more than the battle itself, decided the war. By the summer Antony's forces at Actium were short of food and rowers, deserting in numbers, and his council was split between those who wanted to fight on land in Macedonia and those, led by Cleopatra, who wanted a naval breakout.

events.title: Ahenobarbus deserts Antony
events.summary: Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, Antony's most distinguished Roman supporter and an enemy of Cleopatra, rowed across to Octavian's camp shortly before Actium, already ill with fever; Antony sent his baggage and servants after him. He died within days.

events.title: Herod's Nabataean war and the earthquake
events.summary: Sent by Antony against the Nabataean king Malichus instead of to Actium, Herod was defeated at Canatha, then, after a severe earthquake in spring 31 killed some 30,000 in Judaea (and damaged Qumran), won a victory near Philadelphia (Amman). Absence from Actium let him change sides cleanly.

events.title: Herod meets Octavian at Rhodes
events.summary: Having executed the aged Hyrcanus II as a possible rival, Herod went to Octavian at Rhodes in spring 30, laid aside his diadem, and declared that he had been loyal to Antony and would be as loyal to his new master. Octavian restored his crown and later enlarged his kingdom with Jericho, Gaza and coastal cities.

events.title: Cornelius Gallus takes Paraetonium
events.summary: While Octavian approached Egypt from Syria, Gaius Cornelius Gallus, with Antony's former African legions, seized Paraetonium (Mersa Matruh) and repulsed Antony's attack, during which Gallus drowned out Antony's appeals to the troops with trumpets and destroyed his ships with a harbour chain.

battle.significance: Closed the western approach to Alexandria.

events.title: Death of Caesarion
events.summary: Cleopatra had sent Caesarion, then seventeen, with treasure toward the Red Sea and India; his tutor Rhodon persuaded him to return, and Octavian, advised by the philosopher Areius that 'too many Caesars is not good', had him killed. Antony's elder son Antyllus was dragged from Caesar's statue and executed.

events.title: Diodorus completes his Bibliotheca
events.summary: Diodorus of Agyrium in Sicily completed his forty-book universal history, from mythical times to Caesar's Gallic War, about 30 after some thirty years of work including a visit to Egypt in 60-56, where he saw a Roman lynched for killing a cat. Books 1-5 and 11-20 survive, preserving lost sources such as Posidonius on the Sicilian slave wars.

events.title: Amphitheatre of Statilius Taurus
events.summary: Titus Statilius Taurus, Octavian's general, built Rome's first permanent stone amphitheatre on the Campus Martius from the spoils of his African triumph (34) and dedicated it with gladiatorial games in 29. It burned in the fire of AD 64 and was replaced by the Colosseum.

events.title: Virgil's Georgics read to Octavian
events.summary: Returning from the East in summer 29, Octavian rested at Atella, where Virgil and Maecenas read him the newly finished Georgics over four days, Maecenas taking over when Virgil's voice failed. The four-book poem on farming, trees, livestock and bees had taken seven years and is dedicated to Maecenas.
events.detail: Composed amid civil war, the poem frames hard labour (labor improbus) as the human condition, ends Book 1 with the portents after Caesar's murder, and closes with the myth of Aristaeus and Orpheus. Servius reports that the last half of Book 4 originally praised Gallus and was rewritten after his disgrace, a claim modern scholars mostly reject.

events.title: The doors of Janus closed
events.summary: On 11 January 29 the Senate decreed that the doors of the shrine of Janus Geminus be closed, signalling that Rome was at peace on land and sea, for only the third time in Roman history after Numa and 235 BC. Augustus would close them twice more.

events.title: The trilingual stele of Cornelius Gallus at Philae
events.summary: The first prefect of Egypt, the poet Gaius Cornelius Gallus, crushed a revolt in the Thebaid, received Meroitic envoys and placed a client ruler over the Triakontaschoinos south of Aswan, recording his deeds in Latin, Greek and hieroglyphs on a stele at Philae dated 16 April 29, boasting that he had taken his army further than any before him.
events.detail: Such self-advertisement by a subordinate was exactly what Augustus could not allow; Gallus fell from favour in 27/26 and killed himself. The stele was later broken and reused in a temple foundation. Gallus' four books of elegies to Lycoris made him the founder of Latin love elegy; a papyrus from Qasr Ibrim published in 1979 preserved some ten lines.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Divus Iulius
events.summary: On 18 August 29, during his triple triumph celebrations, Octavian dedicated the Temple of the Deified Julius at the east end of the Forum, on the spot where Caesar's body was burned, its podium decorated with the bronze rams of ships captured at Actium (the Rostra Iulia).
events.detail: The cult had been voted by the triumvirs in 42 under the lex Rufrena; a column and altar first marked the pyre site. The temple contained Apelles' Venus Anadyomene, bought from Cos. It made the Forum's eastern end a monument of the new dynasty, facing the Rostra at the other end, and Octavian's coinage of 36 already showed its design with a star in the pediment.

events.title: Dedication of the Curia Iulia
events.summary: On 28 August 29 Octavian dedicated the new Senate house begun by Caesar in 44 to replace Faustus Sulla's curia, which had been demolished after the fire at Clodius' funeral pyre. He placed in it the statue and altar of Victory from Tarentum, decorated with Egyptian spoils; the altar's removal in 382 became a great pagan-Christian controversy.

events.title: AEGYPTO CAPTA coinage
events.summary: Aurei and denarii of 28 show Octavian's head with a crocodile and the legend AEGYPTO CAPTA, proclaiming the conquest of Egypt, while the cistophori of Ephesus of the same year call him 'champion of the liberty of the Roman people' (LIBERTATIS P R VINDEX). The two messages, conquest abroad and restoration at home, frame the settlement of 27.
scholarship: Sutherland, Roman Imperial Coinage I2 (1984) Augustus 275, 476

events.title: Octavian begins his Mausoleum
events.summary: In 28 Octavian began a huge circular tomb, 87 metres across, on the northern Campus Martius, with public gardens around it. Built during the war with Antony, it was a pointed contrast with Antony's reported wish to be buried in Alexandria. Marcellus was the first to be buried there in 23.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Apollo on the Palatine
events.summary: On 9 October 28 Octavian dedicated the Temple of Apollo next to his house on the Palatine, vowed in 36 against Sextus Pompey on land struck by lightning. Its porticoes of yellow Numidian marble held statues of the fifty Danaids, and its libraries of Greek and Latin literature; the Sibylline Books were later moved to the temple's base.
events.detail: Apollo had become Octavian's patron at Actium, where the god's temple overlooked the battle; the temple's doors showed the Gauls driven from Delphi and the death of Niobe's children. Excavations since the 1950s have revealed painted terracotta plaques of Apollo and Hercules struggling for the Delphic tripod. The complex fused the princeps' house with the sanctuary in a way that anticipated the imperial palace.
